We focus on situational awareness tasks where predictions inherently depend on network-wide spatial relationships through electrical connectivity. Despite extensive research, most ML-based approaches remain system-specific, limiting real-world deployment. This limitation stems from a dual barrier. First, topology changes shift feature distributions and alter input dimensions due to power flow physics. Second, reconfigurations redefine output semantics and dimensionality, requiring models to handle configuration-specific outputs while maintaining transferable feature extraction. Our core insight is treating topology as a learnable dimension through training on diverse reconfigurations, enabling the model to learn universal power flow physics rather than memorizing fixed networks. We achieve this through three synergistic mechanisms: scalar-weight graph convolutions with physics-aware operators handle variable input dimensions and distribution shifts, adaptive pooling maps topology-specific features to unified latent representations, and parallel transformer generates configuration-specific outputs using positional encoding. Our Universal Graph Convolutional Network (UGCN) achieves transferability to any reconfiguration or variation of existing power systems without any prior knowledge of new grid topologies or retraining during implementation. Choices about which entities become nodes, which relationships become edges, and what text each node contains can substantially affect downstream performance. In practice, finding optimal constructions often requires expert knowledge or manual trial and error. We introduce TACO-Graph, a decision tree framework for learning which graph construction choices are most effective for a given dataset and task. Specifically, we focus on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) constructed from multi-attribute tabular data. TACO-Graph enumerates valid TAG representations, scores each using fast proxy evaluation on small representative subsets, and trains an interpretable decision tree on those scores. Across five datasets spanning citation networks, product reviews, and bibliographic relationships, our decision trees predict construction quality on separately drawn evaluation samples with mean Spearman $\\rho$ above $0.9$ for node classification and above $0.8$ for GraphRAG retrieval. Our trees systematically identify which constructions perform better across both GNN and GraphRAG tasks, and the full pipeline is released as an open-source library to support evaluation on new tasks and datasets at https://github.com/AmiriHayes/text_attributed_graphs. propagation characteristics-aware graph neural network with contrastive difficulty guidance for rumor detection","venue":"Journal of Supercomputing","year":2026},{"abstract":"The realm of high-performance computing has expanded to include machine learning tasks of many forms. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are becoming increasingly popular, with their applications expanding across diverse domains. As the scale of graph data continues to grow, including larger numbers of nodes, edges, and higher embedding dimensions, standardized libraries such as DGL and PyG have been developed to facilitate GNN computation. These libraries allow the computation to be described a a high level of abstraction, providing high productivity on the part of the developer. However, with the rapid increase in the number of processor cores and the evolution of multicore architectures, these libraries often show poor scalability and fail to execute GNN inference efficiently on the latest multicore systems, particularly those with upwards of a hundred cores. To address this limitation, we introduce FrontGI, a fast and scalable set of techniques that advances the frontier of GNN inference on large-scale graphs (over 100,000 vertices) by leveraging graph-property- and architecture-aware design. FrontGI employs different parallelization strategies optimized for diverse graph structures, maximizing the utilization of multi-level cache hierarchies in multicore systems. Although existing methods have made substantial progress in intra-domain TF forecasting, inter-domain TF forecasting remains underexplored and faces several fundamental challenges. Specifically, semantic gaps between technologies from different domains hinder effective representation learning; historical inter-domain TFs are highly sparse, limiting the ability to learn reliable structural dependencies; and intra-domain and inter-domain TFs exhibit distinct flow patterns, which are difficult to model within a unified framework. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning (LGCL) framework that supports both intra-domain and inter-domain TF forecasting. Specifically, we first leverage LLMs with bias-aware representation adjustment to generate semantically enriched and accurate technology representations to bridge gaps across multiple domains. Then, to mitigate the sparsity of inter-domain TF data, a technology co-occurrence view is incorporated to complement historical TF information. We further develop a non-negative contrastive learning module to integrate the TF and co-occurrence views, enabling effective representation alignment without relying on negative samples. In addition, we design decoupled loss functions to separately supervise intra-domain and inter-domain flows, mitigating the difficulty of jointly modeling their different flow patterns under a unified objective. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into future technology flow trends. In this paper, we propose Jev-GAD, a training-free generalist graph anomaly detection framework that bridges heterogeneous numerical evidence and pretrained decision mechanisms. To address heterogeneous anomaly patterns, we construct complementary structural, attribute, and neighborhood evidence and transform heterogeneous statistics into graph-relative anomaly percentiles. a hybrid deep learning model with feature fusion attention and dual parallel CNN for drug-target binding affinity prediction","venue":"Journal of Supercomputing","year":2026},{"abstract":"Designing optimal auctions for allocating public infrastructure-such as airport slots and energy resources-is challenging due to interdependent resources and complex side-constraints. While the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction guarantees maximum welfare, it cannot maximize revenue or accommodate the multi-objective trade-offs inherent in public infrastructure systems. We propose a differentiable, constraint-aware framework for combinatorial auction design that enables end-to-end learning of fractionally feasible, approximately strategy-proof mechanisms. Our primary contribution is a combinatorial constraint enforcement technique that ensures fractional feasibility by construction, bypassing the need for penalty-based approximations. We introduce CAGraph, a novel graph-based architecture designed to capture dependencies between items and bidders, alongside CANet and CAFormer as deep learning baselines, for combinatorial settings. We also provide a Matching Pursuit-inspired decomposition that maps fractional allocations to feasible discrete allocations and empirically evaluates the resulting discretization gap. In synthetic benchmarks and an airport slot-divestiture case study, respectively, the learned mechanisms achieve up to 73.5% and 180% higher expected revenue than VCG, under small empirical regret. Finally, we visualize the Pareto frontiers for revenue, welfare, and fairness, providing regulators with a decision-support tool to design infrastructure auctions that balance profitability, efficiency and equity.","already_present":false,"authors":["Mai Pham","Vikrant Vaze","Peter Chin"],"candidate_id":"candidate-c36c345925b43185b2f442af","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"arxiv":"2610.31977","semantic_scholar":"eab9ee1087cb64d6ebec5e47a12bfa0f747940f7"},"identity_key":"arxiv:2610.31977","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/eab9ee1087cb64d6ebec5e47a12bfa0f747940f7","title":"Differentiable Combinatorial Auction Design: Optimizing Revenue-Welfare-Fairness Frontiers With Graph Attention Networks","venue":null,"year":2026},{"abstract":"Spatial multi‐omics technologies jointly profile multiple molecular layers in situ, enabling integrated characterization of tissue organization and cellular states. However, many graph-based approaches remain computationally demanding because they rely on repeated message passing over global graphs, whereas naive local sampling may disrupt cell-level correspondence when multimodal features and graph topologies are not induced synchronously. Moreover, simple concatenation or fixed-weight fusion does not explicitly account for unequal uncertainty between expression‐derived and spatial evidence, making the learned representations sensitive to feature corruption, technical noise and modality inconsistency.\n \n \n \n We present SubPoE, a subgraph-induced Product-of-Experts framework for spatial multi‐omics integration. SubPoE synchronously induces aligned local subgraphs from modality‐specific molecular similarity graphs and a shared spatial graph, preserving molecular‐similarity topology correspondence while reducing per‐iteration graph complexity. Dual‐topology variational graph encoders model expression-derived structure and spatial context as probabilistic experts, which are adaptively fused according to their uncertainty through a Product‐of‐Experts formulation. A composite self-supervised objective further improves robustness and cross‐modal alignment.\n \n \n \n Across eight public paired spatial multi‐omics datasets, SubPoE achieves competitive and comparatively stable performance against existing methods. Ablation, sensitivity, robustness and efficiency experiments further support the contributions of synchronous subgraph induction and uncertainty‐aware fusion.\n \n \n \n These results establish SubPoE as an effective approach for learning topology‐preserving, uncertainty-aware representations of heterogeneous spatial multi‐omics data.","already_present":false,"authors":["Yuan-Fang Li","Wen-Tao Gao","Jun-Hao-Ren-Jun-Hao Ren","Qian-Ran Wei","Xin-Lei Wang","Li-Heng Zhang","Rui-Ting Li","Ya-Dong Wang","Xiao Zhang"],"candidate_id":"candidate-2a65d261fc31cbcf6fdea292","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"doi":"10.3389/fgene.2026.1977260","semantic_scholar":"d85b33b5c685ef448d629eb4e1e07e7b4a569331"},"identity_key":"doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1977260","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/d85b33b5c685ef448d629eb4e1e07e7b4a569331","title":"SubPoE: a subgraph-induced Product-of-Experts framework for spatial multi-omics integration","venue":"Frontiers in Genetics","year":2026},{"abstract":"Manufacturing operators must maintain production while limiting emissions when disturbances spread through shared resources. In contrast, analytical mixed-size placers optimize differentiable full netlist wirelength and density objectives but are typically unaware of thermal effects. We propose EGGPlacer, an energy-guided diffusion framework that incorporates analytical placement feedback and thermal feedback into macro placement generation. An analytical placer acts as an online physical response model, exposing the standard cell distribution and a full netlist wirelength proxy induced by each intermediate macro placement, while a differentiable thermal model provides temperature feedback. These signals are formulated as composable energies and injected throughout reverse diffusion without retraining the underlying generative model. Experiments on public placement benchmarks show that EGGPlacer achieves competitive mixed-size HPWL relative to strong analytical and learning-based macro placers. In the end-to-end evaluation, EGGPlacer also obtains the lowest average routed wirelength and peak temperature among the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate that analytical and thermal guidance provide distinct and complementary benefits across wirelength proxies, routed wirelength, and thermal objectives.","already_present":false,"authors":["Qi Zhou","Guo-Jun Liu","Juan-Hong Zhao","Guang-Zhi Qi","Ze-Hao Chen","Ming Lu"],"candidate_id":"candidate-54364fca714eaf5998590140","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"arxiv":"2610.33099","semantic_scholar":"e8641e4d155b54c7e617c48dd77b7efa73d1d3cf"},"identity_key":"arxiv:2610.33099","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/e8641e4d155b54c7e617c48dd77b7efa73d1d3cf","title":"EGGPlacer: Energy-Guided Generative Chip Placement with Diffusion Models","venue":null,"year":2026},{"abstract":"Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. Nevertheless, the current lane detection algorithms may face difficulties in complex driving situations due to poor visual feature extraction, unstable temporal prediction, and inadequate modeling of structural relations between lanes.\n \n \n \n In order to overcome these issues, this paper introduces the unified spatio-temporal graph learning approach that integrates spatial feature extraction, temporal context aggregation, uncertainty-driven graph formation, graph attention reasoning, and geometric optimization. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Fraud patterns and methods are continuously evolving, with fraudulent transactions often disguised to resemble legitimate activity. Real world transaction data for fraud detection is severely affected by class imbalance making it harder to detect these transactions. Fraudulent transactions are rarely isolated. Accounts, devices, and other common attributes are often shared across fraudulent activity, revealing relational patterns that individual transaction features alone cannot capture. Graph-based approaches model these relationships explicitly. This work presents RGH-GNN, a heterogeneous graph neural network that addresses this limitation by incorporating transaction-level risk scores, generated by a supervised LightGBM classifier as edge weights. The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Mean case-wise RMSE reductions are 9.77%, 17.37% and 3.72% relative to a validation-selected expert, uniform averaging and linear stacking, respectively; gains over stacking concentrate in absolute-risk cases. A matched state-adaptive control yields mean RMSE 0.03460 versus 0.03080 for OSTMF-Net. On a disjoint 2013 chronology on the same feeder, OSTMF-Net records RMSE 0.03067, high-risk F1 0.795 and Top-10 agreement 1.000. Our approach applies cell-specific correction in data integration, generating cell embeddings that align cells across batches while preserving intrinsic cell types and developmental trajectories. However, conveying retrieved graphs through non-unique linear textual contexts to Large Language Models (LLMs) leads to graph-structure degradation and inefficient KV-cache reuse. Meanwhile, graph-structure order optimization is already NP-hard, and the additional KV-cache reuse objective further complicates the search by introducing potentially conflicting orders. To tackle these issues, we propose FuseRAG, a cost-efficient graph-based RAG framework that shifts most retrieved evidence from explicit textual contexts to latent representations. Our main idea is to separate reusable evidence content from query-aware structural interactions in latent space, while retaining only a few explicit facts as semantic anchors. The resulting latent representations are injected into decoder self-attention, where they reshape attention over evidence and thereby influence hidden states and next-token probabilities. This design preserves graph structure through latent interactions, enables evidence reuse beyond exact token-prefix matching. Experiments on three multi-hop question-answering datasets with Llama-3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B show that FuseRAG improves answer quality while achieving up to 2.7x and 2.2x TTFT speedups over the fastest graph-based baseline, respectively.","already_present":false,"authors":["Ting-Qi Wang","Ying-Shu Li","Zhi-Peng Cai"],"candidate_id":"candidate-fa649eac7c8f62b0052e1884","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"arxiv":"2610.22818","semantic_scholar":"c15b96d60f9087d03fcdc8f14a06b49874671820"},"identity_key":"arxiv:2610.22818","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/c15b96d60f9087d03fcdc8f14a06b49874671820","title":"FuseRAG: Fusing Structure and Evidence into Inference for Cost-Efficient Graph-based RAG","venue":null,"year":2026},{"abstract":"Object detection in sports videos holds significant application value in tactical analysis, athlete tracking, and intelligent broadcasting. However, existing methods face two key challenges when processing sports scenes: on one hand, target distribution in sports footage is strictly constrained by field boundaries, yet generic detectors uniformly allocate detection resources across the entire image, causing frequent false detections in off-field regions due to the visual similarity between spectators and athletes; on the other hand, objects such as athletes, balls, and referees in sports scenes form stable spatial co-occurrence patterns governed by game rules, yet existing methods predict each object independently, failing to leverage cross-category relational cues to assist the detection of difficult targets. To address these issues, this paper proposes SportRGDET (Sport Relation-Graph DEtection Transformer), a framework that achieves accurate detection through two core modules: the Scene Prior Guided Module (SPGM) jointly estimates the spatial probability distribution and boundary gradient map of the field region from multi-scale encoder features, fuses them to generate a hierarchical field confidence mask, and performs spatial modulation on the deformable self-attention weights of the encoder, which reallocates attention resources toward the effective field area and progressively suppresses off-field interference across layers, thereby reducing false detections while incurring only moderate additional computation; the Relation Reasoning Enhancement Module (RREM) treats each candidate object as a node during the detection decoding stage, adaptively learns inter-node association strengths through a relation encoder based on category embeddings and relative spatial positions of node pairs, constructs a dynamic relation graph, and bidirectionally propagates contextual information across nodes via graph attention mechanisms, enabling difficult targets to refine their predictions by leveraging positional and categorical cues from surrounding identified objects, enhancing detection robustness under occlusion and blur conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that SportRGDET achieves significant performance improvements on multiple sports detection benchmark datasets, validating the effectiveness of scene prior and relation reasoning mechanisms in sports scene object detection.","already_present":false,"authors":["Qing-Ya Ouyang","Chao-Yi Su","Qing-Yuan Li"],"candidate_id":"candidate-01b4abd2637fe5dd49f47842","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"doi":"10.1371/journal.pone.0348924","semantic_scholar":"aba7360477948d813a54f2a6d84e6e56fbebafa2"},"identity_key":"doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0348924","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/aba7360477948d813a54f2a6d84e6e56fbebafa2","title":"SportRGDET: Scene prior and relation graph enhanced detection transformer for sports scenes","venue":"PLoS ONE","year":2026},{"abstract":"Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on graph-structured data. However, their success heavily relies on the availability of clean labels, an assumption that often fails in real-world scenarios. The learnability of GCNs is intrinsically linked to the neighborhood structure of nodes, making it critical to understand how this structure changes in the presence of label noise. In this work, we investigate how the neighborhood label distribution of a node changes under label noise. We mathematically derive that label noise smooths this distribution, which inherently increases its entropy and severely decreases interclass distinguishability. To address this challenge, we propose Leave-one-out Entropy Node Screening (LENS), an end-to-end framework that identifies noisy nodes by measuring the reduction in neighborhood entropy when a specific node is removed. LENS further incorporates a relabeling mechanism to recover and preserve valuable feature information instead of entirely discarding the identified noisy nodes. Crucially, the end-to-end computational overhead of LENS is remarkably low. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art node classification accuracy while executing an order of magnitude faster than existing noise-robust approaches.","already_present":false,"authors":["Pintu Kumar","N. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.","already_present":false,"authors":["Jan Herschel","A. von Gladiss"],"candidate_id":"candidate-982bfe400a683d3b22e684c2","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"arxiv":"2610.23475","semantic_scholar":"886d28e9d078a546083945e7c9dc3196c9966cf7"},"identity_key":"arxiv:2610.23475","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/886d28e9d078a546083945e7c9dc3196c9966cf7","title":"TAN: A Size- and Form-Adaptive Masked-Convolution Encoder for Tissue Graphs","venue":null,"year":2026},{"abstract":"Train delay heterogeneity between service categories is well known but rarely characterized at large scale from operational data, and rarely used directly to drive the design of graph-based delay-propagation models. This study uses the real International Railway Network Dataset (IRD2025) – 2,678,291 operational records from 3,324 trains across 1,397 stations on the Italian railway network, January–June 2024 – to empirically characterize this delay heterogeneity and to motivate and evaluate a heterogeneous graph-based delay-prediction framework (HTW-STGN).\n \n \n \n Exploratory analysis is conducted on the full real IRD2025 dataset, rather than the smaller synthetic validation sample used in earlier work, to characterize delay heterogeneity across the seven Italian train service categories and to test the empirical assumptions – cross-category delay correlation, weather sensitivity and category-level delay ranking – that originally motivated the heterogeneous-edge design of HTW-STGN. HTW-STGN is implemented as a relation-aware graph-feature aggregation model, with heterogeneous edges (same-category/cross-category) grounded in real, physically observed infrastructure sharing and evaluated on a held-out June 2024 test set.\n \n \n \n Results confirm and correct earlier reported patterns: regional services (96.4% of all records) have lower delays than long-distance categories, the opposite of the result reported from the earlier synthetic sample; the weather effect is real but moderate rather than strongly multiplicative as earlier estimated; and cross-category delay correlation is consistently weak (r = −0.05 to 0.37) rather than the high correlation (up to 0.89) that had originally motivated the choice of heterogeneous graph edges. Only 4.6% of station-to-station links in the network are used by more than one train category, and this real infrastructure-sharing structure – rather than delay correlation – is used to root HTW-STGN's heterogeneous edges. This design reduces mean absolute delay-prediction error by 12% beyond a homogeneous-graph baseline (95% CI [0.49, 0.63] min, p < 0.001) and by approximately 40% beyond features that ignore graph structure entirely, consistently across all seven categories.\n \n \n \n This is the first large-scale empirical characterization of delay heterogeneity across the full real Italian Railway Network Dataset, and the first to test – and correct – the correlational assumptions behind a heterogeneous graph-based delay-propagation architecture using real operational data rather than a synthetic proxy. HTW-STGN's heterogeneous-edge design is re-grounded in observed infrastructure sharing rather than delay correlation, offering a first empirical test of the heterogeneous-edge hypothesis for delay propagation in Italian railways.","already_present":false,"authors":["K. Kumar","Michael Moses Thiruthuvanathan","Babu Kumar Sathiyamurthy"],"candidate_id":"candidate-5148ccddd567e110a3e7ac6e","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"doi":"10.1108/rs-06-2026-0045","semantic_scholar":"876b7cef66acc1a8a197de63f9d54769386ed514"},"identity_key":"doi:10.1108/rs-06-2026-0045","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/876b7cef66acc1a8a197de63f9d54769386ed514","title":"Delay heterogeneity in Italian rail network with exploratory analysis and a proposed heterogeneous spatio-temporal graph framework","venue":"Railway Sciences","year":2026},{"abstract":"The Internet of Things (IoT) interconnects billions of devices that naturally form decentralized graph structures, where edges encode privacy-sensitive interaction patterns. Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely on message passing over these edges, making relational privacy protection a critical concern. To mitigate privacy risks, edge-level differential privacy (DP) has been widely adopted to perturb graph structures. However, existing edge-level DP mechanisms apply uniform perturbation across all edges, disregarding their heterogeneous structural importance. To address this limitation, we propose a personalized edge-level privacy-preserving GNN (PELP-GNN) learning framework, the first personalized edge-level privacy-preserving GNN learning framework, whose key novelty is to assign each edge a differentiated privacy budget according to its structural significance, thereby avoiding the overprotection of low-importance edges and the underprotection of critical ones. Specifically, PELP-GNN estimates edge importance based on forest edge centrality (FEC) and allocates personalized privacy budgets accordingly. Furthermore, it incorporates an adaptive aggregation scheme to mitigate the effects of nonuniform noise during message passing. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that PELP-GNN satisfies $\\epsilon $ -edge local DP (LDP) while providing personalized protection. Unlike existing works, PELP-GNN is a general, plug-and-play framework that can be seamlessly integrated into state-of-the-art edge-level DP-based GNN learning frameworks. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy across varying privacy budgets.","already_present":false,"authors":["Zi-Jun Song","Dian Lei","Yan-Li Yuan","Lie-Huang Zhu"],"candidate_id":"candidate-23f5d8307d957e5da1d08b7c","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"doi":"10.1109/jiot.2026.3721975","semantic_scholar":"0dab363602973fe3d7a9d49f3f2f47a6dd9694e4"},"identity_key":"doi:10.1109/jiot.2026.3721975","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0dab363602973fe3d7a9d49f3f2f47a6dd9694e4","title":"Achieving Personalized Edge-Level Privacy-Preserving Graph Neural Networks on Decentralized Graphs","venue":"IEEE Internet of Things Journal","year":2026},{"abstract":"Cooperative localization (CL) is a key enabler for future cooperative intelligent transportation system applications. By sharing and fusing multisource information, it can provide high-accuracy localization for connected autonomous vehicles in GNSS-denied or limited environments. Practical CL scenarios often involve heterogeneous cooperative nodes, such as vehicles and landmarks, and relative measurements (e.g., range and bearing). However, existing graph neural network (GNN)-based CL methods do not sufficiently account for scene heterogeneity or fully exploit relative information. Moreover, the state components estimated in CL exhibit substantial scale discrepancies, making effective joint optimization crucial for improving the overall estimation performance of the model. To address these issues, a heterogeneous CL Graph Transformer (HCLGT), together with an adaptive optimization strategy, is proposed for the real-vehicle CL task. First, we incorporate edge-based relative position encoding into the attention computation to better leverage relative measurements. Second, we design relation-specific aggregation modules for different measurement relationships and employ node uncertainty to adaptively adjust attention weights, improving robustness under heterogeneous information quality. Finally, an adaptive loss function is developed to dynamically balance the optimization of multiscale state components. The proposed method is validated on the real-world Leibniz University Cooperative Perception and Urban Navigation Dataset (LUCOOP). Experimental results show that, compared with the best-performing baseline, the proposed method reduces the localization RMSE by 44.61%. Extensive experimental analyses further validate the effectiveness of each module.","already_present":false,"authors":["Sheng-Sheng Xing","Hai-Gen Min","Xia Wu","Wu-Qi Wang","Xiang-Mo Zhao","Guo-Qiang Mao"],"candidate_id":"candidate-1759d0ab90fd511ada8523ff","catalog_paper_id":null,"citation_count":0,"external_ids":{"doi":"10.1109/jiot.2026.3720786","semantic_scholar":"dc5cc46d1ade8958a153b1c27d278a58760b3dbe"},"identity_key":"doi:10.1109/jiot.2026.3720786","keywords":[],"node_id":null,"provenance":{"operation":"search","provider":"semantic_scholar"},"relation":"citation","relation_source_node_id":"21041260a5394f42891b020128fa60fa","removed":false,"source_url":"https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/dc5cc46d1ade8958a153b1c27d278a58760b3dbe","title":"Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Connected Autonomous Vehicles' Cooperative Localization","venue":"IEEE Internet of Things Journal","year":2026},{"abstract":"Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) contain complementary diagnostic and laboratory information about patient health. However, irregularity, sparsity, heterogeneity, and incompleteness in documentation complicate EHR modeling. To address the problem, we introduce GraphBEAT (Graph-based Bucketized Event Aggregation over Time), a temporal graph representation learning framework that groups clinical events into time buckets and transforms observed features into patient-specific, temporally directed graphs to enable early risk stratification for gastrointestinal cancers. Each node in an EHR graph encodes feature identity, observed value, and temporal position of clinical events. A context-aware, time-decay message-passing mechanism models transitions between successive buckets, followed by multi-head attention pooling to generate patient-level representations. GraphBEAT was trained and evaluated on multi-site longitudinal diagnosis codes and laboratory tests to predict pancreatic, liver, and intestinal cancer at 12-, 24-, and 36-month diagnostic lead times. In all experimental setups, GraphBEAT consistently outperformed baseline graph neural networks (GraphSAGE, GAT, and GCN) and sequence modeling approaches (Transformer and long short-term memory [LSTM]). GraphBEAT also required over 250x fewer floating-point operations per patient and over 20x fewer parameters than the Transformer and LSTM baselines. candidates.abstract: With the development of the integration of aerial, terrestrial, and satellite networks, Uncrewed Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) serve as a new type of aerial communication platform, playing a key role in Internet of Things (IoT) scenarios. However, multi-hop UAV networks still suffer from energy limits, bandwidth scarcity, dynamic topology, and unstable links. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an edge-cloud communication protocol framework (EC-LLM-MARL) based on Large Language Models (LLMs) and MARL. In this framework, the cloud side constructs a chain-of-thought to guide LLM reasoning, and distilled expert strategies are transferred to UAVs through knowledge distillation and fine-tuning, improving training efficiency and reducing communication overhead. Additionally, a Graph Attention Network (GAT) is employed to extract deep features of observation targets, while Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) is combined with a self-attention mechanism at the UAV end to enhance credit assignment and convergence efficiency in dynamic environments. Furthermore, the framework designs a differentiated reward mechanism for task load balancing among multiple UAVs, improving the scalability of the algorithm in large-scale network scenarios. Extensive simulations show that EC-LLM-MARL significantly accelerates training convergence and substantially outperforms existing methods, achieving a 77% increase in throughput, a 13% rise in coverage, and the highest remaining energy levels.
candidates.title: LLM-Enhanced MARL for Multi-Hop UAV Networking: An Edge-Cloud Protocol Aware Framework

candidates.abstract: Person Re-IDentification (ReID) is vital for public-safety applications, yet camera-based ReID suffers in low-light environments and poses serious visual privacy risks. In contrast, millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar sensing has gained significant attention in ReID due to its ability to perceive human movement patterns by emitting electromagnetic waves, making ReID unaffected by lighting conditions and capable of privacy preserving. However, current radar-based ReID methods are primarily supervised, and radar data is challenging for human eyes to interpret, making annotation extremely difficult and costly. To this end, we propose an unsupervised radar ReID method based on multi-level cross-view mutual signal contrastive learning. First, to drive unsupervised contrastive learning that depends on data augmentations, we utilize signal processing techniques to transform raw radar signals into frequency spectrum and point clouds, and these forms constitute different and complementary augmented versions of the same sample. Second, we construct a multi-level contrastive model between frequency spectrum signals and point clouds through global contrast, cross-view prediction contrast, clustering contrast, and cross-view cluster center contrast, effectively aligning different views and enhancing unsupervised robustness. Additionally, we employ a well-designed local and global graph attention network to learn more discriminative radar point cloud features. Extensive experimental results illustrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing radar-based unsupervised methods.
candidates.title: mmWave Radar-Based Unsupervised Person ReID via Multi-Level Mutual Signal Contrastive Learning

candidates.abstract: With the rapid advancement of mobile technology and ubiquitous computing, spatial crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising computing paradigm. The growing complexity of spatial tasks has increasingly driven the demand for coordination among interdependent tasks and the cooperative participation of mobile workers, which remains relatively unexplored among existing studies. To fill this gap, this paper introduces Dependency-Cooperative Spatial Crowdsourcing (DCSC), a novel problem that explicitly models task dependencies and enables systematic worker cooperation to address complex spatial scenarios. To solve DCSC, we propose a two-stage solution: Dependency-aware Recommendation and Cooperation-aware Matching. In the first stage, we develop a multi-agent reinforcement learning approach enhanced with meta-gradient techniques to recommend suitable subtasks while considering dependency constraints. In the second stage, we propose a genetic algorithm-enhanced game approach to achieve optimal cooperative assignment, guided by a multi-dimensional matching utility function. To ensure consistency and optimization across both stages, we employ meta-gradients from the policy network to guide the optimization of the utility function. Additionally, we utilize graph neural network-based policy clustering to address task heterogeneity, enabling each cluster to learn specialized parameters and enhance reinforcement learning performance. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach.
candidates.title: Efficient Task Assignment in Dependency-Cooperative Spatial Crowdsourcing

candidates.abstract: Addressing distribution shifts between training and testing sets is paramount for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Graph rationale learning has emerged as an effective paradigm to tackle this challenge by extracting invariant subgraphs as rationales for prediction. However, existing methods typically rely on the subgraphs produced by a rationale extractor without explicitly assessing their reliability, particularly during early training stages when the extractor is prone to generating inaccurate or biased rationales. Learning with such unreliable rationales can mislead the classifier and further deteriorate rationale quality, ultimately undermining generalization performance. In this paper, we rethink the objective of graph rationale learning and propose Cooperative Rationale Selection (CoRas), a novel architecture designed to enhance the reliability and robustness of rationale representations. Specifically, CoRas employs a dual-classifier framework to cooperatively select reliable rationales. Motivated by the small-loss criterion, CoRas prioritizes rationales with low prediction loss, while simultaneously selecting rationales with high prediction divergence to mitigate selection bias caused by relying solely on self-predictions during training. This allows CoRas to effectively select reliable rationales for downstream tasks, subsequently enhancing graph rationale learning. Experimental results on both real-world benchmarks and synthetic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CoRas in extracting reliable rationale subgraphs for combating out-of-distribution graph settings in graph classification.
candidates.title: CoRas: Cooperative Rationale Selection for Graph Rationale Learning in Out-of-Distribution Graphs
candidates.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering

candidates.abstract: Modern power grids are increasingly exposed to diverse cyber-physical attacks that originate in the cyber layer and disrupt physical operation. A critical defense challenge is to rapidly determine whether an attack has occurred and identify its type. To address this challenge, this paper aims to develop a generalized detection scheme capable of identifying multiple types of attacks, particularly unknown ones. It is first observed that, under normal operation, cyber-layer data and physical-layer states are consistent across layers and evolve smoothly over time, while attacks disrupt these consistencies. Building on this insight, a self-supervised Cross-Layer Cross-Temporal Contrastive Learning (CL-CTCL) framework is proposed, which employs a Graph Attention Network-Gated Recurrent Unit (GAT-GRU) encoder to capture spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics. Two complementary contrastive objectives are introduced: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) for cross-layer alignment and Information Noise-Contrastive Estimation with Momentum Contrast (InfoNCE-MoCo) for temporal consistency. Residual deviations from these consistencies provide reliable attack fingerprints, enabling detection and classification of both known and unknown attacks. Experiments on an IEEE 118-bus cyber-physical testbed show that the proposed CL-CTCL achieves high accuracy on known attacks and generalizes well to unknown ones, outperforming baseline methods across standard metrics.
candidates.title: Detection of Unknown Attack in Cyber–Physical Power Systems via Self-Supervised Cross-Layer and Cross-Temporal Consistency

candidates.abstract: Deep learning (DL)-based methods have illustrated excellent performance in distribution network fault diagnosis. However, the “opaque” nature of DL models hinders grid operators from understanding the decision-making processes of these models, affecting model trustworthiness and robustness in diversified diagnosis applications. This paper proposes a hybrid attention-augmented self-interpretable channel-grouped graph convolutional network (HASIG) for diverse short-circuit fault diagnosis of distribution networks, including binary fault detection, faulted line identification, and fault type classification. A channel-grouped graph convolutional network is proposed to learn features from three-phase voltage and current measurements. We present a hybrid attention that combines global edge attention and channel-grouped attention, which can augment the critical features with faithful and robust interpretations during model training, enabling users to gain insights into the predictive behavior inside the model. These three short-circuit fault diagnosis tasks are collaboratively trained under a multi-task learning architecture with interpretable loss constraints. Experiments were conducted on the IEEE 33-bus, IEEE 33-bus with distributed energy resources, and IEEE 123-bus systems with randomized fault parameters. The results show that HASIG achieves competitive diagnostic performance and good interpretability, and demonstrates strong robustness under noisy and missing-data conditions.
candidates.title: Hybrid Attention-Augmented Self-Interpretable Channel-Grouped Graph Convolutional Network for Robust Distribution Network Fault Diagnosis

candidates.abstract: This work addresses a fundamental challenge in applying deep learning to network topology-dependent power system applications: developing neural network models that transfer across significant system changes, including networks with entirely different topologies and dimensionalities, without requiring training data from unseen reconfigurations. We focus on situational awareness tasks where predictions inherently depend on network-wide spatial relationships through electrical connectivity. Despite extensive research, most ML-based approaches remain system-specific, limiting real-world deployment. This limitation stems from a dual barrier. First, topology changes shift feature distributions and alter input dimensions due to power flow physics. Second, reconfigurations redefine output semantics and dimensionality, requiring models to handle configuration-specific outputs while maintaining transferable feature extraction. Our core insight is treating topology as a learnable dimension through training on diverse reconfigurations, enabling the model to learn universal power flow physics rather than memorizing fixed networks. We achieve this through three synergistic mechanisms: scalar-weight graph convolutions with physics-aware operators handle variable input dimensions and distribution shifts, adaptive pooling maps topology-specific features to unified latent representations, and parallel transformer generates configuration-specific outputs using positional encoding. Our Universal Graph Convolutional Network (UGCN) achieves transferability to any reconfiguration or variation of existing power systems without any prior knowledge of new grid topologies or retraining during implementation. Experimental results on state forecasting and false data injection detection demonstrate that UGCN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in cross-system zero-shot transferability across both transmission and distribution networks.
candidates.title: Universal Graph Convolutional Network: Zero-Shot Transfer Across Power Grid Topology Reconfigurations

candidates.abstract: Graph-structured representations of text data have become foundational across machine learning, yet it remains unclear how to systematically construct a graph from a given dataset for a target task. Choices about which entities become nodes, which relationships become edges, and what text each node contains can substantially affect downstream performance. In practice, finding optimal constructions often requires expert knowledge or manual trial and error. We introduce TACO-Graph, a decision tree framework for learning which graph construction choices are most effective for a given dataset and task. Specifically, we focus on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) constructed from multi-attribute tabular data. TACO-Graph enumerates valid TAG representations, scores each using fast proxy evaluation on small representative subsets, and trains an interpretable decision tree on those scores. Across five datasets spanning citation networks, product reviews, and bibliographic relationships, our decision trees predict construction quality on separately drawn evaluation samples with mean Spearman $\rho$ above $0.9$ for node classification and above $0.8$ for GraphRAG retrieval. Our trees systematically identify which constructions perform better across both GNN and GraphRAG tasks, and the full pipeline is released as an open-source library to support evaluation on new tasks and datasets at https://github.com/AmiriHayes/text_attributed_graphs. TACO-Graph provides a systematic and interpretable guide for determining how to convert tabular data to text-attributed graphs for downstream tasks.
candidates.title: TACO-Graph: Automated Construction of Text-Atributed Graphs
A graph neural network approach to physical distress screening in subsidized housing

candidates.abstract: The realm of high-performance computing has expanded to include machine learning tasks of many forms. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are becoming increasingly popular, with their applications expanding across diverse domains. As the scale of graph data continues to grow, including larger numbers of nodes, edges, and higher embedding dimensions, standardized libraries such as DGL and PyG have been developed to facilitate GNN computation. These libraries allow the computation to be described a a high level of abstraction, providing high productivity on the part of the developer. However, with the rapid increase in the number of processor cores and the evolution of multicore architectures, these libraries often show poor scalability and fail to execute GNN inference efficiently on the latest multicore systems, particularly those with upwards of a hundred cores. To address this limitation, we introduce FrontGI, a fast and scalable set of techniques that advances the frontier of GNN inference on large-scale graphs (over 100,000 vertices) by leveraging graph-property- and architecture-aware design. FrontGI employs different parallelization strategies optimized for diverse graph structures, maximizing the utilization of multi-level cache hierarchies in multicore systems. We evaluate a number of GNN models with FrontGI on a 128-core AMD EPYC system. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries, FrontGI achieves up to 3.35$\times$, 3.20$\times$, 2.89$\times$ and 3.10$\times$ speedups over DGL for GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, and SGC models, respectively, and even greater improvements over PyG, across a range of large-scale, high-dimensional graph datasets with diverse structural properties.
candidates.title: FrontGI: Architecture-Aware Parallel GNN Inference on Chiplet-Based Multicore Systems

candidates.abstract: A graph neural network (GNN) forecasting a collection of load series combines two mechanisms, sharing parameters across series and reading neighboring series, and a gain over a non-graph model may come from either; telling them apart decides whether a graph is worth maintaining. We propose a model diagnostic protocol that compares the GNN with three reference models: a per-node network, a network shared across nodes without neighbors, and the same GNN without edges. Degree-preserving rewiring tests whether neighbor identity matters. After a tuned benchmark on regional load in France and on low-voltage feeders in the UK, we apply the protocol to deliberately short node histories, as when non-stationary demand leaves only recent observations relevant: the feeders, within one week, and a public dataset of client consumption series. On the feeders, sharing parameters recovers most of the error gap between node-specific models and GNNs, about two thirds against a regularized one. Adding the edges to an otherwise identical backbone brings a smaller gain, half or more of which disappears under rewiring. On the client series, the neighbor mean degrades the per-node model on the shorter window and the edges'gain is not consistently distinguishable from zero; on the regions of France, where each node's own history is already informative, the ranking between per-node models and GNNs changes with tuning. A synthetic study points to noisy local measurements as one regime where neighbors help. In an exploratory online aggregation, graph and non-graph forecasters appear complementary, and the weight assigned to GNNs is not proportional to their contribution. In none of the three datasets do the edges account for most of a GNN's advantage over node-specific models, so a forecasting gain should be credited to the graph only after comparison with per-node and shared references.
candidates.title: A Diagnostic Protocol for GNNs in Electricity Load Forecasting: Separating Parameter Sharing from Neighborhood Access

candidates.abstract: Illicit account detection is a critical task for financial risk control systems, aiming to pinpoint malicious actors within transaction networks. Existing efforts typically recast transaction networks into directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect anomalies via topological structures under the homophily assumption. However, directly grafting GNNs onto transaction graphs is faced with at least two pivotal challenges, i.e., structural inconsistency and label scarcity. The former arises from deceptive connections forged by malicious actors, while the latter stems from the lack of annotated data. In light of these, we introduce MINT, a novel graph neural framework that mitigates structural inconsistency via an attentive message-passing scheme on transaction graphs. Specifically, MINT introduces a discrepancy-aware feature propagation, which tracks malicious actors by quantifying deviations between nodes across bi-directional transaction flows. A transaction salience module is proposed to mitigate structural inconsistency by adaptively regularizing the interaction strength between nodes. Furthermore, to alleviate label scarcity, MINT is optimized via Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, which exploits only a minority of illicit nodes coupled with a majority of unlabeled ones. Extensive experiments conducted on three financial transaction benchmarks, including two large-scale public and one in-house real-world datasets, validate the superior effectiveness of MINT over several cutting-edge baselines.
candidates.title: MINT: Mitigating Structural Inconsistency via Attentive Message Passing for Financial Anomaly Detection

candidates.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in modern machine learning, yet most existing frameworks remain fundamentally static, limiting their applicability in Dynamic Data Driven Application Systems (DDDAS) where observations arrive sequentially under uncertainty. We introduce B-EAGLe (Bayesian Evidence Accumulation for Graph-Based Learning), a probabilistic framework inspired by CBGT-Net (cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic network) that reformulates graph classification as a sequential evidence accumulation process. B-EAGLe combines a GNN encoder with a Bayesian accumulator that incrementally updates posterior beliefs over class labels as new observations arrive, committing to a decision only when sufficient confidence is achieved. Experiments on CIFAR10 demonstrate competitive performance together with principled confidence estimation under sequential observations.
candidates.title: Bayesian Evidence Accumulation for Graph-Based Learning in Dynamic Data-Driven Applications Systems

candidates.abstract: Link prediction remains difficult in sparse graphs, where diffusion heuristics lack connectivity and geometric methods suffer spectral instability when coupling learned representations with diffusion operators. We introduce Concorde, an energy-based framework that resolves this by decomposing link likelihood into three structurally decoupled branches: (i) a parameter-free spectral anchor that establishes permutation-invariant topological stability; (ii) a mixed-curvature residual on a learnable $\mathbb{H}^{d_h}_{c_h} \times \mathbb{S}^{d_s}_{c_s}$ product manifold, regularized by a feature-aware Ollivier-Ricci curvature proxy; and (iii) a continuous vector field on the tangent bundle of hyperbolic space for non-local structural alignment across topological gaps. The branches are fused via learned gating and trained with an N-pair ranking loss aligned with retrieval-style evaluation. Across five benchmarks spanning sparse, dense, featureless, and attributed regimes, Concorde establishes state-of-the-art early retrieval precision, nearly doubling P@10% over leading baselines in sparse settings.
candidates.title: Concorde: Geometry-Aware Link Prediction via Decoupled Energy Minimization

candidates.abstract: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks combine a node's history with information from graph neighbors. The central question is whether graph neighbors provide predictive information beyond each node's own history. Forecast accuracy depends on both the choice of neighbors and the way graph messages enter the temporal model. We study these choices as graph construction and graph exposure on U.S. state unemployment, traffic speed, and electricity demand. Our diagnostic design uses two comparisons: varying exposure while holding the domain graph fixed, and varying construction while holding late gated integration fixed. A GRU using only each node's own history and randomized graph controls help assess what the graph contributes. Under a common change forecasting protocol, the same domain graph can improve or worsen error relative to the GRU across integration designs. Late integration alone is insufficient, while adding a fusion gate yields lower mean error in all three tasks. With late gated integration fixed, a graph based on residual correlations has the lowest mean error among the tested graphs, although randomized graphs perform similarly on unemployment. The findings support evaluating graph construction and integration together, with conclusions tied to the comparisons actually performed.
candidates.title: How Much Graph Is Too Much? Graph Construction and Exposure in Spatio-Temporal Forecasting

candidates.abstract: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.
candidates.title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction

candidates.abstract: On million-node graphs, the memory wall arrives before the compute wall: a GNN that never fits in VRAM cannot deliver the all-node inference its accuracy promises. The standard remedy, pruning, has always been an accuracy tax - paid once and never refunded. DPR refuses this framing. Its central insight is that the mask that shrinks training can also scaffold recovery: one compact node set bounds both computations of graph learning, serving as the encoder's training graph and, at inference, as the anchor from which a sparse structure-aware decoder rebuilds every pruned node (double-layer sparsification). The order is inverted - prune for efficiency, then reconstruct for accuracy - and the tax is repaid: the deployed 30%-budget model trains in 1,450 MiB of peak memory on one 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating a same-GPU rerun of the edge-sparsification baseline DSpar by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory; against the same-protocol full-batch no-prune encoder the deployed point pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax for a 2.8x smaller training footprint. Pruning without reconstruction leaves the encoder at 0.378 within the same 40-epoch window (Fig. 4), and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE, giving up approx. 5.4 pp of test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB of peak training memory; extended variants (long-range context, external text features, a CAN-bus application) are reported as extensions and do not compete with the deployed method, and the 41.8%-budget M4 point, scored on a coarsened super-node graph with its own split, is reported separately rather than compared with the original-node baselines. DPR thus turns aggressive node pruning from an accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator for VRAM-limited all-node inference.
candidates.title: Decoupled Prune-and-Reconstruct: Training on a Compact Core with Double-Layer Sparsification

candidates.abstract: Correlated corroboration can make knowledge-based systems overconfident when dependent reports are treated as independent evidence. This paper presents an influence-aware evidence aggregation architecture that makes source dependence explicit and constrains confidence growth under partial dependence knowledge. The architecture combines an influence-indexed evidence graph (EIIG), a generalised estimate of effective independent evidence (EIE) with graded dependence weights, and a bounded confidence-propagation rule (CONFPROP). We evaluate the architecture against three baselines—naive independence aggregation, a Bayesian independence update, and a source-discounted comparator—across four controlled synthetic scenarios and a semi-realistic external case study using 500 claims from the FEVER fact-verification corpus. Under the strongest synthetic dependence regimes, CONFPROP consistently reduces confidence inflation relative to naive aggregation: inflation ratios are 4.00 in a common-parent echo-chamber scenario and 10.00 in a fully duplicated cascade, while no suppression occurs when evidence is genuinely independent. A factorial sensitivity analysis across 648 parameter combinations per stress-test scenario confirms that the discount factor γ decreases with the diversification threshold K and increases with the unknown-status weight α. The architecture provides deterministic, auditable confidence updates with structured monitoring signals, and is designed for modular integration into existing knowledge-based systems operating under uncertain source dependence.
candidates.title: Echo chamber dynamics and influence aware evidence aggregation for epistemic integrity in knowledge based systems

candidates.abstract: Graph Neural Networks are widely used to learn structural representations of relational data. Hierarchical graph pooling learns multi-level representations by progressively coarsening graphs; however, prior methods rely on predefined cluster numbers or fixed pooling ratios, limiting adaptability to individual graphs. We propose Graph-Dependent Pooling (GDPool), which dynamically determines pooling granularity for each graph. We analyze optimization conflicts among layer-wise objectives through gradient alignment, showing that independently supervised pooling levels can send conflicting gradients to shared parameters. GDPool uses self-attention to select graph-specific anchors representing structurally important nodes and constructs coarse graphs through soft node assignment. Experiments on metal-organic framework and molecular graph benchmarks show that GDPool consistently achieves the best predictive performance across all benchmarks. Evaluations using modularity and the effective number of clusters show that GDPool achieves consistently higher modularity than existing methods while the number of active clusters decreases monotonically with depth. Sensitivity analyses confirm stable behavior across hyperparameter and architectural choices.
candidates.title: Graph-dependent pooling: adaptive granularity in hierarchical graph neural networks

candidates.abstract: Before every neutral objective in professional League of Legends, each team decides which of its five players walk to the pit, which hold a lane, and when to commit. The leading analysis of such setups, TAGNet for Counter-Strike 2, clusters graph-network embeddings of player positions and reads cluster win rates as tactical quality. We treat a setup as an allocation on a walled map: formations are set partitions on the lattice $\Pi_5$, control is a geodesic Voronoi split of a navigation graph, and commitment is an allocation game solved as a quantal response equilibrium priced in win probability. On all 164 games of MSI and Worlds 2025 (2,994 team-setups, minimap tracks validated against Riot positions), trailing teams leave the pit empty far more often than leading teams, by +34.8 percentage points at the first baron and +30.4 percentage points at Atakhan. Our model, HASSE-QRE, finds six setup patterns that whole-model series-bootstrap refits reproduce (ARI 0.819, comparable to 0.813 for TAGNet's $K$-Means step alone) and indicates that teams price fights, travel and committed players, not the objective itself (weight 0.018; fixing it to one costs 59.9 log-likelihood points). The equilibrium reproduces a quarter of the commitment gap, almost all of it through state variables rather than its strategic channels. Weighting a team-level contrast by exposure moves it across $p=0.05$ (0.046 against 0.052). We release the tracks, setups and code.
candidates.title: Allocation Before the Clock: Graph, Set and Game Theory of Professional League of Legends Objective Setups

candidates.abstract: The classification of research papers from different academic data is still challenging due to the presence of semantic ambiguity, lack of information, fluctuating credibility, and complex linkages across research articles. Existing fuzzy graph neural networks depend too much on membership information and cannot truly consider the intuitionistic uncertainty, trust dependability, and structural importance of nodes at the graph propagation level. To overcome these constraints, this paper presents an intuitionistic fuzzy graph neural network architecture that combines trust-aware intuitionistic representations and a unique node Laplacian energy mechanism. The suggested Node Laplacian Energy is derived from the graph Laplacian's row-wise norm and is used as an adaptive node-weighting metric to assess each research paper's local structural contribution. Furthermore, a diffusion-based propagation technique is used to enhance information transmission across semantically linked publications and capture larger graph relationships. The suggested system is tested for research-paper categorization with semantic similarity features and intuitionistic fuzzy credibility information. Its performance is compared to known machine learning and graph neural network baselines utilizing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The findings show that including uncertainty-aware representations, structural node weighting, and diffusion-based graph propagation can improve discriminative academic content categorization. The suggested paradigm offers a unified way to model semantic linkages, uncertainty, believability, and graph structural relevance in research-paper categorization.
candidates.title: An energy-aware diffusion graph neural network based on intuitionistic fuzzy credibility graphs for research-paper classification

candidates.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-target affinity (DTA) is a core technical step in high-throughput drug screening and targeted drug discovery, which directly affects the efficiency of candidate compound mining and the control of research and development costs. Traditional experimental methods are difficult to meet the requirements of high-throughput screening, while existing deep learning-based models generally suffer from bottlenecks such as shallow fusion of multi-source heterogeneous features, insufficient mining of interactive features, and inadequate generalization robustness. To address these issues, we propose HAFI-DTA (Hierarchical Attention-Guided and Feature Iterative Interaction for Multimodal Drug-Target Affinity Prediction). Specifically, our framework employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to guide the fusion of multi-source heterogeneous features, and combines a two-layer GRU with iterative interaction to capture the deep correlations among features. Experimental results on the KIBA and Davis datasets demonstrate that the proposed HAFI-DTA model achieves overall performance comparable to the current state-of-the-art, while delivering stable and modest improvements in both CI and MSE metrics. Moreover, under the most challenging drug–target double cold-start scenario, our model attains the best performance, exhibiting excellent generalization robustness. In addition, interpretability analysis shows that the model can automatically focus on the key residues of the real binding pockets of proteins, providing an important basis for subsequent drug design and binding mode research.
candidates.title: HAFI-DTA: an interpretable multimodal framework for drug-target affinity prediction based on hierarchical attention guidance and feature iterative interaction
GD-GAT: a robust dam displacement prediction framework integrating spatial priors and gated graph attention network

candidates.abstract: This study presents a novel data-driven methodology for extraction causal chains from high-dimensional climate datasets, with a particular focus on detecting and visualizing the pathways that link climate anomalies across geographically distant regions. The proposed framework is designed to be computationally efficient while maintaining high interpretability, making it suitable for large-scale analytical applications in climate science. To assess its effectiveness, the methodology is applied to the well-studied teleconnection between the El Niño—Southern Oscillation and precipitation variability in Northeastern Brazil—a region highly susceptible to climate extremes such as droughts. The approach integrates clustering method, causal inference technique, and optimized path selection algorithm to construct interpretable causal chain graphs. Results demonstrate the methodology’s strong capability to identify key causal relationships and reproduce known climate phenomena. By effectively managing complex and massive climate data, this methodology contributes to the advancement of data science tools for climate analytics and offers valuable insights for understanding global climate teleconnections.
candidates.title: A multivariate causal chain detection methodology assessed on the ENSO modulation of the Northeastern Brazil precipitation
candidates.venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analysis

candidates.abstract: Accurate probabilistic forecasting of geographically distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation is challenged by incomplete measurements, weather-dependent cross-site correlations, and quantile crossing. This study proposes a physics-guided framework that integrates a physics-informed Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (PIL-WGAN-GP), a dual-exploration spatiotemporal graph neural network (DEST-GNN), and an arbitrary-quantile recurrent decoder (AQ-RNN). The imputation module combines self-supervised masking, solar geometry, a clear-sky-based power envelope, and deterministic projection. The forecasting module fuses a static spatial prior with a time-varying dependency graph, while the decoder predicts aggregate PV quantiles directly through bounded positive spacings and monotone interpolation. The framework was evaluated in a retrospective case study using hourly PV generation records from 11 Belgian regional PV zones and matched meteorological records in 2025. For 3-, 6-, and 12-h consecutive gaps, PIL-WGAN-GP reduced normalized mean absolute error from 1.450%, 2.473%, and 5.252% for linear interpolation to 0.869%, 1.027%, and 1.300%, respectively. Hard projection eliminated nighttime leakage and upper-envelope violations. Across 1-, 6-, 12-, and 24-h horizons, DEST-GNN-AQ reduced the average daylight nMAE from 3.689% for the no-graph AQ-RNN to 3.509%, with the main gains occurring at 6–24 h. The model generated nested 50%, 70%, 80%, and 90% prediction intervals with a zero quantile-crossing rate. Their empirical coverages were 41.72%, 62.81%, 69.84%, and 85.26%, indicating that structural validity was achieved while calibration remains improvable. Collectively, these findings validate the proposed framework’s ability to bridge physically admissible data reconstruction with reliable, non-crossing probabilistic forecasting for PV clusters.
candidates.title: Physics-guided non-crossing probabilistic forecasting for distributed photovoltaic clusters using dynamic graph attention

candidates.abstract: This study focuses on the spatiotemporal prediction of supply chain finance risk contagion and constructs a model based on the dynamic graph attention diffusion mechanism for in-depth exploration. The risk-aware dynamic graph attention network (DyGAT) is used to model the time-varying network structure of supply chain finance, where the spatial attention weight α_ij(t) is updated adaptively at each time step by integrating real-time risk intensity signals to realize real spatiotemporal coupling modeling. A bounded diffusion mechanism with natural risk attenuation is introduced to characterize the propagation process of risks in spatial and temporal dimensions, avoiding unbounded cumulative defects in traditional formulas. Methodologically, a supply chain finance dynamic graph structure is constructed by integrating multisource data such as historical transaction data and corporate financial information, with clear data cleaning, fusion and feature engineering processes, and the model is trained, validated and ablated strictly. The results show that the model can effectively predict the spatiotemporal paths and topological characteristics of supply chain finance risk contagion and identify key nodes and critical periods of risk propagation, and the ablation experiment verifies that the dynamic attention module and bounded diffusion module bring 18.2% and 12.5% precision improvement, respectively. It provides strong support for financial institutions and supply chain enterprises to formulate risk prevention strategies in advance and is of great significance for improving the stability and resilience of the supply chain finance system. However, caution is needed when applying the model to small-sample settings, as the limited sample size may constrain its generalizability to other industries and regions.
candidates.title: Research on the spatiotemporal prediction of supply chain finance risk contagion based on a dynamic graph attention diffusion mechanism

candidates.abstract: Technology flow (TF) forecasting aims to predict whether a technology will be utilized by another, which is significant for future cross-integration technology innovation. Although existing methods have made substantial progress in intra-domain TF forecasting, inter-domain TF forecasting remains underexplored and faces several fundamental challenges. Specifically, semantic gaps between technologies from different domains hinder effective representation learning; historical inter-domain TFs are highly sparse, limiting the ability to learn reliable structural dependencies; and intra-domain and inter-domain TFs exhibit distinct flow patterns, which are difficult to model within a unified framework. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning (LGCL) framework that supports both intra-domain and inter-domain TF forecasting. Specifically, we first leverage LLMs with bias-aware representation adjustment to generate semantically enriched and accurate technology representations to bridge gaps across multiple domains. Then, to mitigate the sparsity of inter-domain TF data, a technology co-occurrence view is incorporated to complement historical TF information. We further develop a non-negative contrastive learning module to integrate the TF and co-occurrence views, enabling effective representation alignment without relying on negative samples. In addition, we design decoupled loss functions to separately supervise intra-domain and inter-domain flows, mitigating the difficulty of jointly modeling their different flow patterns under a unified objective. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into future technology flow trends. Our code is available at https://github.com/huijieliu2023/LGCL.
candidates.title: LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning for Technology Flow Forecasting

candidates.abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify irregular entities in graph-structured data, yet heterogeneous anomaly patterns and distributional differences across graphs challenge generalizable detection. Existing training-free approaches avoid task-specific optimization but primarily rely on predefined numerical scoring rules, leaving the semantic interpretation of heterogeneous anomaly evidence largely unexplored.
